title: Python IO threadpool -> worker handoff: sampling notes
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from a week of profiling short/medium requests that showed an odd knee in p95 latency when we scale concurrency on CPU-only nodes. Hypothesis refined: most of the p95 regression is happening during handoff from async IO accept/recv to the Python worker threadpool + tokenization path, not in transformer token decode itself. This doc captures sampling traces, microbench shells, and possible mitigations.

Why this matters:
- Small payload requests (prompt ~20 tokens) dominate our real traffic for many customers; per-request fixed CPU cost matters more than per-token generation cost.
- Observed ~2–6ms extra tail overhead at higher concurrency that we couldn't explain with kernel scheduling alone.

Environment / repro notes:
- AWS c6i.4xlarge (16 vCPU) serving-runtime image: rwinf/runner:2024-11-05
- Python 3.11.4, CPython build with PGO off, GIL default
- uvloop + aiohttp accepting HTTP/1.1 requests, then handoff to ThreadPoolExecutor for CPU-bound preproc/tokenization and model worker queue.
- Tokenizer: HuggingFace tokenizers (rust binding) 0.13.3, fallback to python tokenizer for some models.
- Workload: synthetic client sending 50–200 req/s with concurrency up to 64, payload size 200–800 bytes.

Instrumentation used:
- py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python server
- perf + flamegraph (perf record -F 99 -p PID && perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded)
- system tap sampling for futex/wake events (low fidelity but good signal)
- strace -f -c for a few requests to capture syscalls

Key experiment variations:
- baseline: single-threaded request handling (no ThreadPoolExecutor), tokenization inline
- async-handoff: aiohttp reader -> submit to ThreadPoolExecutor (default behavior)
- pre-tokenize-cache: pretokenize incoming prompts in hot path (cache key: prompt hash)
- ujson vs std json: to check small parsing cost

Observations (sampling summaries):
1) py-spy CPU hotspots showed: accept/epoll_wait -> asyncio.Task switching -> ThreadPoolExecutor._work_queue.get -> <tokenizer rust call> -> memory copies in Python bytes->str conversion. At p95 the expensive chain often had "futex_wait" frames and "_queue_get" frames around handoff.

2) perf flamegraph for high concurrency showed higher stack density in sched_yield/futex contended region than in tokenizer native functions. In other words, lock contention / scheduling between threads accounted for ~25–40% of extra cycles at tail.

3) strace (sample) highlighted repeated recvfrom/read calls followed by short pauses before we see python-level work. Timing suggested that the accept/recv path finishes quickly, then there is a scheduling gap ~200–800us before the worker thread runs. At 64 concurrent clients these gaps accumulate into higher p95.

4) JSON parsing (std json) is small but measurable for tiny payloads (~80–150us). Switching to ujson reduced this by ~30–40us, but did not remove the tail. Tokenizer itself (rust) often took 0.5–1ms for the small prompts, so pre-tokenize cache gave wins when prompts repeated.

Microbench commands used (copy to repro):
- py-spy: py-spy record -o /tmp/pyspy.svg --pid <PID> --subprocesses --native
- perf: perf record -F 99 -p <PID> -g -- sleep 30; perf script | ~/flamegraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded; ~/flamegraph/flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg
- cProfile quick: python -m cProfile -o prof.out run_small_client.py; snakeviz prof.out
- futex sampling: sudo perf record -e futex:* -p <PID> -- sleep 20

Detailed trace examples (abbreviated):
- Request A (single-shot): time recv 120us -> submit executor 80us -> worker scheduled after 600us -> tokenizers::encode 800us -> model request 35ms.
- Request B (high concurrency): recv 110us -> submit 90us -> wait on _work_queue.get (avg wait 900us, tail 3ms) -> tokenization 900us -> model.

Root-cause candidates (non-exclusive):
- A: ThreadPoolExecutor queue wakeup latency: using Python queue + condition variables leads to extra futex wakes and kernel scheduling overhead when many producers/consumers operate.
- B: GIL switching overhead on frequent short tasks: many short CPU tasks cause thread churn and frequent GIL reacquisition/handovers.
- C: Buffer copies at handoff boundary: converting incoming bytes to Python str/bytes before handing to tokenizer causes memory traffic and transient allocations under GIL.
- D: Event loop scheduling policy + task placement: worker threads on same core or remote cores leading to cache thrash; kernel may starve workers when accept path is IO-bound.
What reduced tail in quick tests:
- Batching small prompts into a single tokenization call (batch size 8) reduced per-request overhead by ~25% at p95. Downsides: increases per-request latency for singletons, complexity.
- Using a single long-running consumer thread per worker group and feeding via lock-free queue (atomic ringbuffer in C extension) reduced futex events visible in perf and improved p95 by ~30% in microbench.
- Pre-tokenize caching (LRU 4096 entries) helped heavily for customers with repeated prompts, reducing mean and tail by 0.5–1ms for that workload slice.

Things tried that had minimal effect:
- Replacing std json with ujson (small win for median, negligible on tail).
- Pinning threads to cores (taskset) — small improvements but not practical at scale and brittle across tenants.

Open experiments to run next:
- Replace ThreadPoolExecutor with a thin C extension that implements a lock-free ringbuffer + wake-on-write to avoid futex storms (prototype exists in PR #842). Measure perf and py-spy.
- Try running tokenizers in a dedicated small process pool (multiprocessing with shared-mmap for input) to move tokenizer work out of GIL domain and reduce Python thread churn. Trade-offs: IPC cost, cold-start of processes.
- Microbenchmark: synthetic kernel scheduling test using N producers/consumers to reproduce futex wake density and verify theoretical scaling of condition variable approach vs lock-free.

Action items / proposal:
- Short term: enable pretokenize cache behind a feature flag for Hosted API customers where prompt repetition is high. + switch to ujson for parsing to shave medians. (Owner: Maya)
- Medium term: Merge PR #842 (lock-free ringbuf handoff) into canary image and run canary for 2 weeks against low-latency customers. (Owner: Samir)
- Long term: re-evaluate Python-only handoff for small requests. Consider a hybrid model where small requests are handled via a fast-path C extension or moved to a tiny dedicated worker process pool. (Owner: Eng-Serving-Runtime)

Risks/notes:
- C extension reduces futex but increases maintenance surface and could complicate private/on-prem builds (requires compilation). We need CI coverage for that path.
- Process-pool approach memory cost (per-process tokenizer state) could negate wins for model-hosting nodes with many tenants.

Questions for the team:
- Do we have telemetry to show fraction of unique prompts (to estimate cache hit rate) at customer level? If yes, what's the distribution?
- Are there customers who explicitly require single-thread inline tokenization (policy)? If so, feature flags needed.

Appendix: quick toy to reproduce thread handoff jitter (python):
```
# toy_handoff.py (not production)
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import socket

executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=32)

def cpu_task(b):
    # simulate small CPU tokenization
    s = b.decode('utf-8')
    return len(s)

sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET)
sock.bind(('127.0.0.1', 6000))
sock.listen()

while True:
    conn, _ = sock.accept()
    data = conn.recv(4096)
    # mimics aiohttp handoff: submit to thread pool
    future = executor.submit(cpu_task, data)
    # intentionally not blocking here
    conn.sendall(b'ok')
    conn.close()
```

Notes: run multiple clients with small requests and sample with py-spy or perf to see queue wait frames.

Bottom line:
- For small requests the dominant tail source is scheduling + handoff overhead between async IO thread and Python worker pool. Tokenizer work is not free, but optimizer wins are largest if we reduce futex/wakeup/scheduling churn. The lock-free handoff prototype looks promising. Next steps: run it in canary and measure real p95 with production traffic profile.
